questions.question_text: This disorder is more common in girls.
What is the prevalence rate of enuresis among 5-year-old boys?
questions.explanation: The point prevalence figures for enuresis cited in the DSM-IV-TR are 7 percent of boys and 3 percent of girls at 5 years of age, decreasing to 3 percent of boys and 2 percent of girls by 10 years of age[cite: 6]. Only 1 percent of boys still wet at age 18 years of age, and still fewer girls wet at this age[cite: 6]. The DSM-IV-TR also cites a spontaneous remission rate of between 5 and 10 percent per year after 5 years of age[cite: 6]. Secondary enuresis may occur at any time, but it most commonly begins between 5 and 8 years of age[cite: 6].

options.text: The majority of enuretic children wet intentionally.
There is a correlation between enuresis and psychological disturbance that increases with age.
Children with enuresis are no more likely to have developmental delays than other children.
There is no evidence for a genetic component to enuresis.
Children living in socially disadvantaged environments do not have an increased incidence of enuresis.

correct_answer.text: There is a correlation between enuresis and psychological disturbance that increases with age.

correct_answers.text: There is a correlation between enuresis and psychological disturbance that increases with age.

questions.explanation: There is a correlation between enuresis and psychological disturbance that increases with age[cite: 6]. Additionally, there is increasing evidence for the role of physiological factors in enuresis[cite: 6]. Although the DSM-IV-TR definition of enuresis includes both voluntary and unintentional wetting, the vast majority of enuretic children do not wet intentionally[cite: 6]. Bladder control is achieved gradually and is influenced by neuromuscular and cognitive development, as well as by emotional factors and toilet training; difficulties in one or more of these areas may delay acquisition of urinary continence[cite: 6]. There is also accumulating evidence for a genetic role in enuresis; one large study found that a child’s risk of being enuretic was increased 5.2 times if the mother had been enuretic as a child and 7.1 times if the father had been enuretic[cite: 6]. Additionally, the concordance rate is higher in monozygotic than in dizygotic twins, and 75 percent of enuretic children have a first-degree biological relative with enuresis[cite: 6]. A small minority of children with enuresis wet intentionally; these children often manifest oppositional defiant disorder or a psychotic disorder[cite: 6]. Children living in socially disadvantaged circumstances and children experiencing significant psychosocial stress have a greater incidence of enuresis than other children[cite: 6]. The behavioral disturbances that co-occur with enuresis are quite variable and nonspecific and may represent either coincidental rather than causal correlations with enuresis[cite: 6]. Children with enuresis have significantly higher rates of developmental delays than nonenuretic children, including both children in psychiatric clinic populations and normal control subjects[cite: 6].

questions.question_text: To make a diagnosis of enuresis in an 8-year-old child who wets the bed, at least how often must the child wet the bed?
questions.explanation: To make a proper diagnosis of enuresis in an 8-year-old child using the tenth edition of the International Classification of Diseases (ICD-10), the child must wet the bed or otherwise intentionally or unintentionally void urine inappropriately at least once a month[cite: 6]. In children younger than 7 years old, they must void their urine, intentionally or unintentionally in an inappropriate manner, at least twice a month[cite: 6]. These symptoms must persist at least 3 months with no evidence of a nonpsychiatric medical condition, such as epilepsy[cite: 6]. Also, there must be no evidence of any other psychiatric disorder that meets the criteria for other ICD-10 categories[cite: 6].

questions.question_text: Before issuing a diagnosis of enuresis, a urinalysis must be done to rule out which common condition?
questions.explanation: Because urinary tract infections can produce enuresis, a urinalysis should be part of every evaluation[cite: 6]. Using radiographic procedures with contrast media to detect an anatomical or physiological cause for the enuresis is more problematic because the procedures are invasive and painful, and the diagnostic yield is low[cite: 6]. A large study carried out in a pediatric primary care setting found a 3.7 percent incidence of obstructive lesions in children with enuresis[cite: 6].

options.text: The vast majority of enuretic children experience spontaneous resolution of the problem.
Medications are generally the first step in the treatment of childhood enuresis.
Psychotherapy is never indicated as part of the treatment of enuresis.
The success rate for behavioral interventions is nearly 40 percent.
Classical conditioning methods (bell and pad) are ineffective in children with concomitant psychiatric disorders.

correct_answer.text: The vast majority of enuretic children experience spontaneous resolution of the problem.

correct_answers.text: The vast majority of enuretic children experience spontaneous resolution of the problem.

questions.explanation:
The natural history of enuresis is significant because it impacts treatment decisions, insofar as enuresis is a self-limiting disorder that will eventually spontaneously remit[cite: 6]. Diagnosis is not made until age 5 years to account for children who undergo toilet training at a later stage in the accepted age range (2 to 5 years of age)[cite: 6]. The prevalence of enuresis is relatively high between the ages of 5 and 7 years and then substantially declines[cite: 6]. By age 14 years, only 1.1 percent of boys wet once a week or more, and very few persist into adulthood with the problem[cite: 6].
Behavioral and pharmacological treatments have well established efficacy in treating patients with enuresis, but medications are not the first line of treatment given the risks of side effects and high likelihood of recurrence of the problem when the drugs are discontinued[cite: 6]. Psychotherapy is often useful for ameliorating behavioral disturbances that often accompany enuresis, especially secondary enuresis; however, studies indicate that psychotherapy alone does not tend to have a high success rate in the treatment of patients with enuresis[cite: 6].
A comprehensive review of several studies determined the success rate for behavioral treatment of enuresis to be 75 percent (not 40 percent)[cite: 6]. The primary method of behavioral treatment is the bell and pad method of conditioning[cite: 6]. A pad is placed on the bed with a wire connected to a bell[cite: 6]. When the child wets, the moisture completes a circuit in the pad, ringing the bell and waking the child[cite: 6]. With repeated use, the child learns to awaken before wetting occurs[cite: 6]. This treatment is equally effective in children with and without concomitant psychiatric disorders[cite: 6].

options.text: No significant relationship exists between encopresis and enuresis.
Fewer than 25 percent of children with encopresis have constipation.
Psychological factors are often relevant when encopresis occurs after a previous period of fecal continence.
The symptom must occur at least once weekly for 3 months as part of DSM-IV-TR criteria for the diagnosis of encopresis.

correct_answer.text: Psychological factors are often relevant when encopresis occurs after a previous period of fecal continence.

correct_answers.text: Psychological factors are often relevant when encopresis occurs after a previous period of fecal continence.

questions.explanation: Encopresis may be precipitated by stressful life events; when the disorder begins after a prior sustained period of fecal continence, the behavior may represent a regression precipitated by stressors such as birth of a sibling, parental separation, or the start of school[cite: 6]. A significant relationship exists between encopresis and enuresis; the two disorders commonly co-occur[cite: 6]. Encopresis involves a complicated interplay between physiological and psychological factors[cite: 6]. Inadequate or inappropriate toilet training, ineffective sphincter control, and a variety of emotional reasons may all contribute to the development of the disorder[cite: 6]. Regardless of the origin of the symptom in a given individual, bowel functioning tends to be disturbed: up to 75 percent of children with encopresis are constipated and have excessive fluid overflow[cite: 6]. The DSM-IV-TR specifies one event per month for at least 3 months as part of the criteria for encopresis[cite: 6].

questions.question_text: Tim, age 6 years, was referred to the clinic by his pediatrician because of persistent soiling. Tim’s mother reported that he had never gained control of his bowel habits. After a febrile illness at age 2 years, he developed constipation and required laxatives and suppositories as treatment. After this episode, there was an alternating pattern of constipation, when he did not move his bowels for several days, and diarrhea, when he soiled his pants many times a day. At age 4 years, he again took laxatives for a period of time, and his stools became softer and more regular. His mother began to toilet train him at that time. He was made to sit on the toilet each evening until he “performed.” Although he usually managed to produce a tiny amount of stool during these sessions, he continued to soil his pants frequently during the day. This pattern continued until the time of referral. Tim himself had been distressed about his soiling since starting school, fearing that others would notice when he stained his clothes or when he smelled after a soiling episode. He was anxious when sitting on the toilet in the evenings and insisted that his mother stay in the bathroom with him. He was also enuretic at night. He became dry by day at age 3 years but continued to wet at night; because waking him at night had not prevented his wetting, his mother still put him in diapers to sleep. Apart from the problems of soiling and wetting, his mother believed that Tim was a normal little boy who was happy and outgoing. His developmental milestones were all a little behind those of his older sisters. He sat at 7 months, walked at 18 months, and spoke his first words at about 18 months as well. questions.explanation:
Encopresis is defined by DSM-IV-TR as a pattern of passing feces into inappropriate places, whether the passage is involuntary or intentional[cite: 6]. The pattern must be present for at least 3 months; the child’s chronological age must be at least 4 years[cite: 6].
Enuresis is the repeated voiding of urine into clothes or bed, whether the voiding is involuntary or intentional[cite: 6]. The behavior must occur twice weekly for at least 3 months or must cause clinically significant distress or impairment socially or academically[cite: 6]. The child’s chronological or developmental age must be at least 5 years[cite: 6].
Conduct disorder is an enduring set of behaviors that evolves over time, usually characterized by aggression and violation of the rights of others[cite: 6]. Conduct disorder is associated with many other psychiatric disorders, including attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder, depression, and learning disorders, and it is also associated with several psychosocial factors such as low socioeconomic level; harsh, punitive parenting; family discord; lack of appropriate parental supervision; and lack of social competence[cite: 6]. The DSM-IV-TR criteria require three specific behaviors of the 15 listed, which include bullying, threatening, or intimidating others and staying out at night despite parental prohibitions, beginning before 13 years of age[cite: 6].
Hirschsprung’s disease, also known as congenital megacolon, is congenital dilation and hypertrophy of the colon caused by an absence (aganglionosis) or marked reduction (hypoganglionosis) in the number of ganglion cells of the myenteric plexus of the rectum[cite: 6].
Schizophrenia in prepubertal children is exceedingly rare; it is estimated to occur less frequently than autistic disorder[cite: 6]. In adolescents, the prevalence of schizophrenia is estimated to be 50 times that in younger children, with probable rates of one to two per 1,000[cite: 6].

questions.question_text: More likely to have developmental delays and associated enuresis
questions.explanation: In both enuresis and encopresis, the distinction between primary and secondary has bearing upon the likelihood of associated psychopathology[cite: 6]. One study of 63 boys found that boys with primary encopresis were more likely to have developmental delays and associated enuresis, and those with secondary encopresis were more likely to have experienced high levels of psychosocial stress and to have been diagnosed with conduct disorder[cite: 6].

questions.question_text: Psychopharmacological intervention for this disorder often provides symptomatic improvement but is of limited utility as relapse tends to occur as soon as the drug is withdrawn.
questions.explanation:
Both enuresis and encopresis are three to four times more common in boys than girls[cite: 6]. Several medications have been used with some success in the treatment of enuresis[cite: 6]. Imipramine (Tofranil) has U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA) approval for the treatment of children with enuresis on a short-term basis[cite: 6]. However, tolerance typically develops within 6 weeks of beginning treatment, and relapse at former frequencies of wetting predictably occurs after discontinuing the drug[cite: 6]. Desmopressin (DDAVP), an antidiuretic hormone available in intranasal spray form, is useful in preventing enuresis while being used, but it also does not seem to maintain its effect after discontinuation[cite: 6]. Thus, behavioral techniques are the first line of treatment for children with enuresis[cite: 6]. For treatment of encopresis, combined behavioral and family intervention is the recommended treatment[cite: 6]. Accurate evaluation of the patterns of encopresis is necessary for successful treatment[cite: 6]. The degree to which the child is aware of the passage of feces is significant as well[cite: 6]. If encopresis is a behavior through which the child expresses anger or attracts negative parental attention, the treatment approach is altered[cite: 6]. Psychopharmacological interventions are not typically part of the treatment of encopresis, although they may be indicated in cases of chronic constipation to regulate stool consistency and improve bowel regularity[cite: 6].
Although structural abnormalities are rare causes of enuresis or encopresis, physiological factors are important contributors to both conditions[cite: 6]. For example, children with encopresis who have chronic constipation and overflow incontinence are often found to have abnormal sphincter contractions[cite: 6]. Physiological characteristics, some of which are likely heritable, also contribute to enuresis: 75 percent of children with enuresis have a first-degree relative with enuresis[cite: 6]. Furthermore, children with enuresis are twice as likely to have concomitant developmental delay as other children[cite: 6].
Bowel control is established in 95 percent of children by the fourth birthday and in 99 percent of children by the fifth birthday[cite: 6]. At age 7 years, the frequency of encopresis is 1.5 percent in boys and 0.5 percent in girls[cite: 6]. The prevalence of enuresis declines with age: 82 percent of 2-year-olds, 49 percent of 3-year-olds, 26 percent of 4-year-olds, and 7 percent of 5-year-olds have enuresis[cite: 6]. To be diagnosed as having enuresis, a child must have a chronological or developmental age of 5 years; the cutoff for encopresis is a chronological or developmental age of 4 years[cite: 6].
